<reason>Both sides were sharp and well-structured, and CON deserves credit for the most original move in the debate: recasting disclosure as a notice-and-consent shield and an opportunity cost against substantive limits. But CON's route to victory ends up resting on two things PRO successfully dented. First, when pressed by A3.1, CON honestly conceded that nothing in the motion forbids passing substantive rules too, and retreated to a political-economy prediction about who "holds the pen." That is a legitimate but contingent, unverifiable argument, and it leaves the motion as written largely unopposed on its own terms. Second, the "certificate of regularity / standard of care" harm was asserted as legal mechanics without much grounding, and PRO's reply — a shaded filing manufactures evidence against the firm, while silence can never be false — was a clean asymmetry CON answered only by re-invoking its preferred counterfactual regime. CON did land real damage: B2.3 correctly showed that a cause standard with the burden on the employer does not strictly presuppose disclosure, and the Goodhart turn on PRO's own "quotas are posted on walls" concession was excellent. PRO's rejoinder (entry powers locate the door, not what is behind it; you cannot subpoena or bring a pattern claim against a system nobody must name; prospective/systemic vs. retrospective/lawyer-dependent enforcement) kept the precondition argument alive in its strongest form, and the credit-report analogy went essentially unanswered. CON also carries a small execution cost for a clipped rebuttal that lost its concluding weighing sentence. Net: PRO kept the cleaner, on-motion decision rule intact while CON's harms remained speculative and its crowd-out objection was self-limited to sequencing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's B2.3 — showing that prohibitions with inspectorate entry powers and a "prove cause before a tribunal" standard do not require the employer to admit anything — was the sharpest single strike, because it attacked PRO's load-bearing claim that all substance presupposes disclosure. PRO's most decisive counter was the pairing of A4.2 ("entry powers locate the door, not what's behind it — you need to know what to subpoena") with A5.3's "silence can never be false," which turned CON's shield theory into an argument for at least some documented record.</best_rebuttal>
